text:
Predicting what GM Brad Holmes and the Detroit Lions do come draft time can be sort of a moot exercise. Each year, pundits take a look at the depth chart, attach the Lions to a prospect in that range based on the position he plays and file their mock draft without a second thought. And each year, Holmes and company reside in their office, chuckling over some of the names they’re linked to.

It’s a tale as old as time, and with the draft kicking off Thursday, expect more of the same.

Until then, here’s one final attempt at trying to predict where the Lions might go at No. 17.

Positions of need to monitor

The Lions, of course, don’t draft for need. But there is structure involved. They’ve drafted for need when it aligns with their board, which was the case in 2024. And you can often find them drafting for future needs, like they did a year ago when they selected Tyleik Williams to take over for DJ Reader in 2026.

With that in mind, it’s best to take a 50-foot view of this thing.

Offensive line: The Lions have two offensive line starters locked in for 2026 — center Cade Mays and right guard Tate Ratledge. The rest hasn’t been finalized. Is Penei Sewell making the switch to left tackle? The Lions signed Larry Borom in free agency, and Holmes is on record saying his best film is as at right tackle. A move like that could also open the door for the Lions to draft a young tackle in the first round. And while the Lions could let Christian Mahogany and Miles Frazier battle it out for the left guard spot and hope for development, what if a potential star is there?

Edge: The Lions have D.J. Wonnum slated to start at edge opposite Aidan Hutchinson, but it’s no secret they could use more. The front office has a type — players who can set a physical edge in the run game and win rushes consistently — but that could limit the number of true fits they’d select with Day 1 or 2 capital, as it has in past years.

Safety: If the Lions add a safety on Day 1 or 2 (or early Day 3), it could be viewed as a hedge on the health of Kerby Joseph (knee) and Brian Branch (torn Achilles). In the event those two return to form, though, adding a starting-caliber safety with nickel flexibility could give the team an intriguing trio.

Linebacker: The Lions could use a linebacker now that Alex Anzalone is off to Tampa Bay, but what kind of linebacker? If they’re looking for a true one-for-one replacement in terms of skill set, they could be in the market for an athletic linebacker with the potential to develop into a strong coverage backer. There are a few on Day 2 and 3 who’d make sense.

Defensive tackle: The Lions lost Roy Lopez, and Reader isn’t expected back at this point. That’s a lot of muscle lost in the interior. And while Williams should take a step forward and Levi Onwuzurike will be returning from a torn ACL, could the Lions add another interior defensive lineman? Whether they go for a run-stuffing nose tackle, a pass-rushing three-tech or a combination, it would make sense to add another DT in either the draft or free agency.

Cornerback: Between Terrion Arnold’s name linked to an armed robbery/kidnapping case involving his friends, and D.J. Reed entering Year 2 of a three-year contract, could the Lions make it work with a first-round cornerback? Don’t be surprised.

Best first-round fits

Penn State G Vega Ioane: Arguably the best guard in the class, Ioane would give the Lions a Pro Bowl-caliber guard to slot in next to Sewell at left tackle (if he moves there). His film prep and no-nonsense demeanor would make him a strong culture fit. I was sold when I heard him at the combine. Poised, confident and in control.

Utah T/G Spencer Fano: Fano’s ability to offer quality play at either right tackle or left guard is incredibly enticing. While he projects as an NFL-ready right tackle, he could easily move to left guard for the 2026 season if the Lions believe Borom is one of their best five linemen. That positional flexibility could be the difference between him and another option. I wouldn’t be surprised if they go up to get him. One of my favorite prospects in the class, and a no-brainer if he’s there at 17.

Auburn edge Keldric Faulk: I’ve been on record for months now saying the Lions are going to have a hard time passing on Faulk if he’s available. He’s everything they’ve wanted in an edge rusher opposite Hutchinson. He’s long, powerful, versatile, mature, defends the run at a high level and has an excellent work ethic. He’s one of the younger prospects in the class and his upside is well worth the selection of a No. 17 pick.

Tennessee CB Jermod McCoy: Holmes wouldn’t draft a player coming off a torn ACL in the first round, would he? Surely that’s never happened before, right? One of the most gifted players in the class, McCoy should be on folks’ radar. The medicals will be key here, as it’s possible he slides like Will Johnson in 2025. But the talent is undeniable.

Georgia OT Monroe Freeling: A former five-star prospect, Freeling has tools for days and comes with the frame of a built-in-a-lab left tackle. One of the most athletic tackle prospects in relative athletic score history, Freeling will need time to develop, but his upside is immense. Starting to think he could be there at No. 17.

Clemson OT Blake Miller: In terms of pure culture fit, there might not be a better one than the Lions and Miller. When I heard the story about him delaying wrist surgery during spring practice to be available to his teammates, I knew he instantly checked that box. Then he tested and recorded an RAS of 9.90. Factor in his size, his 54 career starts and his character, you get a perfect fit.

Alabama G/T Kaydn Proctor: Proctor’s fit with the Lions is more of a stylistic one than anything. Players of his size aren’t supposed to move the way he does. Alabama lined him up at receiver on more than one occasion. He’s so young and still scratching the surface of what he could ultimately become, and projects as a mauling guard or a sturdy right tackle, if he keeps his weight in check and continues to develop. Will he ever get there? That’s a big if, but he could in the right situation.

Oregon S Dillon Thieneman: One of the cleanest evals in the draft, Thieneman is an elite athlete with a high IQ to boot. If he’s on the board at No. 17, he could check the BPA requirement as a do-it-all safety with positional versatility.

Toledo S Emmanuel McNeil-Warren: If the Lions are looking for a safety capable of creating game-changing plays, McNeil-Warren could be staring them down at 17. He’s mastered the art of the peanut punch and his versatility and physicality would be welcomed in this secondary.

Oregon TE Kenyon Sadiq: A tight end? In the first round? Again? The Lions, on a mission to add talent without locking themselves into specific positions, take the best player available. Sadiq could join forces with Sam LaPorta to create the most feared TE room in the NFL. Or he could replace him. LaPorta is entering the final year of his contract and watched his 2025 season end with back surgery. A move like this would be a fascinating wrinkle to that discussion.

My guys

Day 1: Ioane, Fano, Faulk, McNeil-Warren, Miami’s Ahkeem Mesidor, UCF’s Malachi Lawrence, Missouri’s Zion Young.

• I’m of the opinion that Lawrence sneaks into the first round. The more I’ve dug into his film, the more I question why he’s been mocked as a second-round pick. He’s got everything you want out of a first-round edge prospect. Size, arm length, speed, athleticism, a refined rush package and effort vs. the run.

• Meanwhile, Young’s violent nature should endear him to NFL teams, no matter where he lands.

• I just really love McNeil-Warren’s game. Think he’s going to help a defense immediately and his ability to get the ball on the ground is something that’s easier said than done. He does it. Consistently.

• I understand the concerns with Mesidor’s age, but it doesn’t bother me. He’s ready to go. I’m just not sure if the Lions will view him as a fit.

Day 2: Illinois edge Gabe Jacas, Pitt LB Kyle Louis, Texas Tech LB Jacob Rodriguez, Miami DB Keionte Scott, Arizona’s Treydan Stukes, Auburn edge Keyron Crawford, Georgia Tech G Keylan Rutledge, TCU S Bud Clark, Michigan edge Jaishawn Barham, Oklahoma’s Gracen Halton.

• If you’ve been following my draft coverage, you know that Louis is a favorite of mine. I really think his success will depend on where he goes, and it’ll take a smart defensive coordinator to find the right role for him, and the Lions have one in Kelvin Sheppard. He has the makings of a quality big nickel/weakside linebacker hybrid.

• Crawford simply hasn’t gotten enough love this cycle. Maybe it’s because he’s overshadowed by Faulk, but Crawford is a more refined pass rusher right now. He could be a steal for a team on Day 2.

• Barham would be a strong fit as a Sam linebacker in Detroit’s system — the hybrid linebacker/edge position. He could really grow into it over time. He intrigues me.

• If the Lions want to wait on a guard rather than taking Ioane, Rutledge could be their guy in the second. A true all-around guard with immediate starter written all over him.

• There are a ton of quality defensive backs there for the taking on Day 2, but my favorite is Scott. He reminds me so much of Devon Witherspoon — without the outside cornerback flexibility. He’s older at 25, but in the second round, that’s a player worth adding without hesitation.

Day 3: TCU LB Kaleb Elarms-Orr, Missouri DT Chris McClellan, Penn State RB Kaytron Allen, Utah TE Dallen Bentley, SF Austin CB Charles Demmings, Oregon LB Bryce Boettcher, Washington CB Ephesians Prysock, Iowa Edge Max Llewellyn, Kansas State DB VJ Payne.

• Day 3 is a good area to attack depth and add special teams contributors. Don’t sleep on the Lions adding a TE or a DB on this day. A ton of depth at those positions in this class.

title: The Jets did a lot of work on the 2026 NFL Draft QBs. Did they find one who fits?
description:
To recap: Between Geno and Geno, the Jets drafted five quarterbacks after the first round.
Still, the Jets have done work — a lot of work — on the rest of the top quarterbacks in this class in hopes of determining if any are worth drafting and developing.
The benefit of drafting a quarterback after Round 1 is that the Jets wouldn’t feel as obligated to play him as a rookie.
Reich is a former NFL quarterback who has been an offensive coordinator or head coach in the NFL since 2013, and he was a quarterbacks coach before that.
Any quarterback the Jets might look at after the first round is going to have flaws — some of them severe.
text:
FLORHAM PARK, N.J. — If a quarterback drafted after the first round is a scratch-off lottery ticket, then the New York Jets have gone through a lot of losing tickets over the years.

They don’t have a rich history of drafting quarterbacks beyond Round 1 — though, they don’t have a rich history of drafting them in the first round either.

Thirteen years ago, the Jets drafted Geno Smith in the second round out of West Virginia. And now, 10 years after he departed at the end of a disappointing and tumultuous tenure, he’s back for another shot at leading the franchise.

Ten years ago, general manager Mike Maccagnan drafted Christian Hackenberg out of Penn State in the second round; he never played a snap for the Jets. Neither did Tajh Boyd, drafted in the sixth round in 2014 out of Clemson. Nor did James Morgan, a fourth-round pick out of Florida International in 2020. Jordan Travis was a sixth-round pick out of Florida State in 2024 — he retired in 2025 due to injuries, without ever even logging a practice in the NFL. Bryce Petty threw four touchdowns and 10 interceptions in 10 games after the Jets picked him as a fourth-rounder out of Baylor in 2015.

To recap: Between Geno and Geno, the Jets drafted five quarterbacks after the first round. They threw a combined 245 NFL passes, all by Petty.

That doesn’t offer much inspiration for a Jets franchise that appears to be on the brink of once again buying a scratch-off ticket and hoping for the best. Just because it hasn’t worked before doesn’t mean it isn’t worth trying again.

This is one of the stranger quarterback draft classes; the consensus is that only one QB has a first-round grade — and that quarterback (Fernando Mendoza) is already locked in as the No. 1 pick. Still, the Jets have done work — a lot of work — on the rest of the top quarterbacks in this class in hopes of determining if any are worth drafting and developing.

The benefit of drafting a quarterback after Round 1 is that the Jets wouldn’t feel as obligated to play him as a rookie. Many have tied the Jets to Alabama’s Ty Simpson — the consensus No. 2 quarterback in this class — simply because the Jets don’t currently have a long-term solution at the position and Simpson is viewed as a caliber of player who could become that solution one day.

Maybe the Jets believe that, though the knocks against Simpson (lack of size, inexperience, lack of arm strength) make it unlikely they’d use one of their current first-round selections (No. 2 and No. 16) on him. More likely, if he’s still there at No. 33 or 44, they’d consider him.

Whether they want him or not, the Jets have done extensive work on Simpson, just as they have on many other notable quarterbacks in this class. The Jets attended Simpson’s Pro Day at Alabama in March. Then a group of top Jets decision-makers — general manager Darren Mougey, head coach Aaron Glenn, offensive coordinator Frank Reich and quarterbacks coach Bill Musgrave — took him out to dinner and conducted a private workout the following morning.

At the NFL’s league meeting a few days later, Mougey said that “it was a good visit” with Simpson.

Over the course of the last few weeks, the Jets have also:

• Had dinner with Carson Beck in Miami prior to his Pro Day.

• Conducted a private workout with LSU’s Garrett Nussmeier.

• Hosted Penn State’s Drew Allar for a private workout.

• Met “extensively” with North Dakota State quarterback Cole Payton, according to a report, and hosted him on a top-30 visit.

• Spoke at length with Arkansas’ Taylen Green at the Senior Bowl and NFL Combine — and likely more since.

• Formally interviewed Behren Morton at Texas Tech’s Pro Day and hosted him for a top-30 visit.

And that’s just the information that has been unearthed.

For the quarterbacks who had private workouts with the Jets — most notably Simpson, Nussmeier and Allar — it is a true job interview. Mougey said the Jets will send the player a “kind of test” the night before and tell them to learn “all of this information,” the GM said.

The next morning, with Mougey, Glenn, Reich, Musgrave and the quarterback in a room, they quiz the player to see how much he retained from the night before.

The goal, said Mougey, “Let’s see how natural it is for you to talk football. Let’s see if we connect in the room personality-wise. And we’ll go through that meeting in the room, talking a lot of football, a little personal stuff, but a lot of their habits, just really getting a feel for their football mind, and then you go out into the field. Obviously, you see them physically, but at the same time, you’re kind of testing them mentally again.”

Glenn said at the owners’ meetings that he watches the quarterbacks during those workouts from the perspective of a defensive coach.

“If I’m a defensive player, how would I defend him? What are the issues we feel like he’ll have?” Glenn said. “Then we try to put him through drills. For example, we had one of our coaches, when one of our QBs drop back I want to attack him and see how he can maneuver in the pocket to get himself free to deliver the ball. Those are some things defensively I want to see.”

The flip side of that, Glenn said, is thinking from an offensive perspective — and evaluating the quarterbacks on the small details of things like how they handle dropbacks, three-step, five-step, under center, play-action and ball handling.

Glenn and Mougey are also leaning heavily on the expertise of Reich and Musgrave. Reich is a former NFL quarterback who has been an offensive coordinator or head coach in the NFL since 2013, and he was a quarterbacks coach before that. Musgrave has been a respected QB coach in the NFL across various franchises since 1997.

“It’s been great,” Mougey said. “Both Frank and Coach Musgrave were on the tour with us and got to go see some of these quarterbacks and it was awesome. Obviously, Frank and Billy have been around a long time, have evaluated a lot of quarterbacks, so there’s been a lot of good discussion.”

Glenn handed the keys to the offense to Reich when he hired him this offseason, allowing him to focus on calling plays on defense. So it would be fair to assume Mougey will be leaning on Reich for his opinions about this quarterback class and how they might fit into his offense.

Back in 2020, when he was coaching the Colts, Reich laid out five specific traits he looks for in quarterbacks, which is something to keep in mind when evaluating whom the Jets might pick this year at the position — if they pick anyone.

1. Toughness, mental and physical.

2. Accelerated vision. “That’s my wording for: How fast do you think on your feet?”

3. Accuracy: “You have to be really accurate in this league. The windows are small.”

4. Footwork: “You have to look for the feet. Most sports are played from the ground up. So as a quarterback, that’s really important, how you play with your feet.”

5. Intangibles: “The leadership. Are you a playmaker in big moments?”

So, considering those traits, which quarterbacks make the most sense for the Jets?

Simpson actually grades out well regarding those traits:

1. He played through injuries in 2025, though those injuries were a detriment to his performance.

2. In terms of “accelerated vision”, The Athletic’s Dane Brugler wrote that Simpson had a proclivity for holding onto the ball too long and second-guessing himself, often leading to sacks.

3. He only completed 64.5 percent of his passes in 2025, though his receivers did drop 25 passes, per Pro Football Focus.

4. NFL.com wrote that Simpson has “exceptional” footwork.

5. Simpson’s inexperience could work against him when it comes to intangibles — there’s not a big enough sample size to understand how he’ll handle himself when the games matter. And he struggled in the College Football Playoffs.

As for the others:

Garrett Nussmeier: He is lauded for his toughness and competitive edge, and Brugler wrote that he has “NFL-quality intangibles” as a leader. He completed 67.4 percent of his passes in 2025. He had the seventh-fastest average time to throw in 2025 (2.48 seconds, per PFF). Nussmeier does well under pressure and isn’t so much inaccurate as he is a gunslinger who is very willing to take risks. He has the zip to squeeze passes into tight windows, which sometimes leads to ill-advised throws while trying to make something happen.

Drew Allar: He has the size (6-foot-5, 228) that Reich typically prefers at quarterback, his arm strength is a plus and he’s well-respected by teammates, but he fell short in some of Reich’s other categories in college. Brugler wrote that Allar has “messy footwork,” “streaky ball placement,” “inconsistent rhythm,” and that he “sabotages himself with late decision-making.” He only completed 63.2 percent of his passes in four years.

Carson Beck: He also has the size (6-4, 233), significant experience (43 starts) and a history of being accurate (69.5 percent completions). Though he doesn’t have ideal arm strength, tends to struggle when his first read isn’t there, turns the ball over a lot (24 interceptions over the last two years), fumbles a lot (17 fumbles) and Brugler wrote that his “ball placement and decision-making plummet when eyes speed up and he gets flushed from original spot.”

Cole Payton: He is an inexperienced (13 starts) quarterback from an FCS school who has tantalizing athleticism (4.56 40, 40-inch vertical), a strong arm and is lauded for his toughness and leadership. Brugler also wrote that Payton has “inconsistent mechanics,” “gets frazzled under pressure” and has “underdeveloped pocket awareness.”

Taylen Green: He is another freak athlete — at 6-5 and 227 pounds, he ran a 4.36 40 and had a 43.5-inch vertical jump. He throws with legitimate arm strength and zip and was respected by teammates for his toughness and leadership. But he also has a funky delivery and inconsistent accuracy (60.1 percent completions, 35 interceptions in 53 games).

Any quarterback the Jets might look at after the first round is going to have flaws — some of them severe. They wouldn’t make it out of the first round if they were perfect.

The question is: Would the Jets put in all of that work into studying this quarterback class if they didn’t plan on drafting one?

title: 2026 NFL Draft: Why Carnell Tate 'No Doubt' Is the Best WR in the Class | FOX Sports
description:

text:
They tore the helmet off his head, but they couldn’t get the ball out of his hands. Two Wisconsin defenders could not stop Carnell Tate, who stood up and screamed in the end zone after catching a 33-yard touchdown pass to start Ohio State's 34-0 rout of the Badgers last October.

It was a touchdown that, technically, Tate shouldn’t have scored.

It should’ve been fellow OSU receiver Brandon Inniss’ TD. And yet when Inniss went down with an injury, then-Buckeyes offensive coordinator Brian Hartline did not hesitate to move Tate into the slot — just for one play — to make sure the execution was perfect. And that’s a testament to Tate, not just because the execution was perfect, but also because …

"He never practiced that play," Hartline, now the head coach at South Florida, told me earlier this month. "He may have seen it in practice, and he saw the other guys do it. But then you put him in the game and competitive excellence. The ball goes his way. He makes a huge play. So that's him as a player. He's always reliable to be put in the big spots."

Tate played in the slot during his freshman year in 2023, seizing an opportunity to get on the field after star receiver Emeka Egbuka suffered an injury. But since that point, Tate has been a perimeter receiver, which was why he hadn’t practiced that play prior to scoring the touchdown.

"Coach [Ryan] Day was like, ‘Hey, what do we do? Brandon's down. Where do you put who?’" Hartline recalled. "And I just said, ‘Listen, put Carnell in the slot. He'll know how to do it. He’ll do a great job on the route. We're good. Stay with the call.’ … We got a coverage that was good for us, and he went up and made a huge play over some defenders for a touchdown."

Tate is prepared for big spots — even when he shouldn’t be.

That’s one of many positive qualities the team that drafts the 6-foot-2, 192-pound receiver will get. But whichever team wants him the most, it'll surely have to be picking in one of the top 10 spots on Thursday night.

"I do it all," Tate told me in Portland at the Adidas "Pro Day" in March. "I run [routes], I block and I catch the ball. I run routes to get open at the highest level. I make contested catches, make good catches over the middle, and I go over top of people. Also, I add to the run game as well. I can impact the game with or without the ball."

Is he the best receiver in this year’s draft?

"Yessir. No doubt," Tate told me.

No hesitation whatsoever.

"I think it’s because of those things [I just mentioned] and also because of more of that," he added. "I feel like I'm the most intelligent receiver out there as well."

Though Arizona State's Jordyn Tyson is emerging as potentially the No. 1 receiver in this year’s class, it’s not all that controversial for Tate to stake his claim. And it's no surprise who Hartline is backing, calling Tate "by far the best receiver in this draft."

Ironically, Tate wasn't the WR1 at any point during his Buckeyes career. Ohio State bestowed that honor to Jeremiah Smith in 2025 and in 2024 and to Marvin Harrison Jr. in 2023. Egbuka was also firmly in the mix with more than 1,000 receiving yards in 2022 and 2024.

"[Tate] really wanted to be the guy. All the guys do," Hartline told me. "When you have a lot of guys in those rooms, sometimes it really makes you a better player when you understand the whole philosophy and where the ball goes. But I think he grew a ton as a person."

You can see the way Tate progressed simply by looking at the raw counting stats. He jumped from 18 catches, 264 yards and one touchdown in 2023 to 52 catches for 733 yards and four touchdowns in 2024. Then in 2025, he had 51 catches for 875 yards and nine touchdowns. It’s not staggering production. But his teammates never took him for granted.

"He’s a big-time receiver who’s gonna make a big play every day," Ohio State All-American edge Arvell Reese told me.

Tate’s draft prospects are a reminder of just how impressive he was in college — despite never being the top target. At Ohio State, that made for tough conversations when he battled to rise even into a WR3 spot in his sophomore year. Hartline and Tate spoke often about how to make it all work.

"I think that there's a lot of honesty. … I'm not gonna lie to the guys. And so if I tell you you're on track, and you just trust me on it, then that's the case," Hartline told me when asked how he managed Tate’s expectations. "I want everyone to have everything, because then there's no hard conversations. But ultimately, he was on pace. Keep trusting the process and the rest will take care of itself."

He added: "Happens all the time, right?"

Not to everyone.

It’s mostly true for the Ohio State locker room, which is a big reason why Hartline is set to start his first season as the head coach for USF. Before Smith, Tate, Egbuka and Harrison Jr., there was Jaxon Smith-Njigba, Garrett Wilson and Chris Olave. Hartline has continued to produce elite pass-catchers, with Tate appearing to be next in line.

This OSU assembly line has created a pro-ready mentality. Not only will these players sharpen each other’s skills off the field, but they’ll have the self-assurance and self-discipline to fight their way to the top of a pro-caliber depth chart.

"They're surrounding themselves with great players, and although frustrating, it's going to be frustrating in the league too. Better get ready for it," Hartline said. "So understanding that, we always want more [production], but that's not how this works. They do a really good job at our job description on each individual play."

Whether Tate lands in Cleveland, Kansas City or any of the other top-10 slots, he'll have to beat out tough competition for a top starting spot. But there's little doubt he'll do just that. He'll do what it takes to make an impact, even if that means jumping into a position he's never practiced — and on the play that matters most.

text:
Everton defender Jarrad Branthwaite is unlikely to play again this season after sustaining a hamstring injury in Sunday's Merseyside derby defeat.

The centre-half was in tears as he left the pitch on a stretcher in the 87th minute of Everton's 2-1 loss to Liverpool at Hill Dickinson Stadium.

After the match, the 23-year-old was seen leaving on crutches and Everton boss David Moyes said he was concerned the injury "could be serious".

Branthwaite missed the first five months of the season - having hamstring surgery in October - and returned to the side in January.

However, his latest injury is unrelated and a scan shows he does not require an operation, Everton said.

He will now start his rehabilitation at the Toffees' Finch Farm training ground, the club added, external.

The injury is a blow to Branthwaite's World Cup hopes, as England's tournament starts on 17 June against Croatia in the United States.

He made his senior debut in a friendly against Bosnia-Herzegovina two years ago but missed out on the Three Lions' 26-man squad for Euro 2024.

text:
Yes, he is raw. Yes, he will have growing pains. But the most exciting thing about Iheanachor as a prospect is that you can easily see how he has progressed in his few short years of playing football, and there is no reason to think that progression will stop. I think Iheanachor has the highest ceiling of any offensive tackle in the class, and if he hit's that ceiling, the Browns will be set for a decade or more.

Round 2 – Pick 39: D'Angelo Ponds, CB Indiana

This is my draft crush. This is my Draft Day, "D'Angelo Ponds no matter what." This kid is an absolute star. Yes, let's get it out of the way, he's 5'9 if he's wearing tall cleats and only 180 pounds. Does that give me pause here? Not even for one second. Go watch the hell he put Jeremiah Smith through. Go watch what he did to Denzel Boston. Look at what he has done to the cream of the crop receivers he has lined up across from all season long. There's no way this kid's size will impair his abilities because his abilities are flat out elite. His cover skills are elite. His ball skills are even better. And then you throw in his return abilities, and D'angelo Ponds instantly makes the Browns a better team.

Round 3 – Pick 70: Germie Bernard, WR Alabama

Since the beginning of the draft season, I have said that I want the Browns to wind up with 2 receivers after their first 4 picks, and Bernard would be a really

solid grab here in the third round.

Bernard brings much of what I love about Carnell Tate to the table. He's a crisp, savvy route runner, he's a smart player in reading a defense and always being where he needs to be, and he's about as sure-handed as it gets, dropping only 4 balls on 232 career targets. He does lack the physicality and strength of Tate, which is why he's available at this point, but while Tate is going damage on the boundaries, Bernard gives you a reliable threat who thrives over the middle of the field.

Put Tate on the outside and interchange Jeudy and Bernard on the other side and in the slot and you have dramatically improved your wide receiver room heading into next season.

Round 4 – Pick 107: Jalon Kilgore, S South Carolina

No, this isn't the true centerfielder type safety prospect the Browns have long searched for, but Jalon Kilgore gives the Browns something else they covet dearly – he is one of the most versatile defensive backs in this class. Kilgore has been a standout player for a couple years now in the SEC as a player that South Carolina basically just designed a position for.

He spent some time as a free-ranging safety in certain situations, and his ability to read a quarterback really stood out. In other situations, he was asked to be abox safety, and his physicality and brutal playing style stood out. And in other situations he was asked to slide to nickel, and his coverage skills and ability to win at the point of attack stood out.

The point is, no matter where Jalon Kilgore was playing, he stood out. That's the kind of player I want rounding out the Browns secondary.

Round 5 – Pick 146: Eli Raridon, TE Notre Dame

As the Browns continue to revamp their tight end room, they find a player built in the mold of what they're searching for in Raridon out of Notre Dame. The 6'6" 250 pounder once again adds that versatility we often see Andrew Berry attracted to. Raridon can line up as the in-line tight end, but he has incredible athleticism,

speed, and explosiveness to get off the line and make big plays in the receiving game. While his skinny-ish frame may scare some people in the run-blocking area, he's been a very good run blocker throughout his career.

Really, the biggest concern about Raridon may be the fact that he tore his ACL his senior year in high school, and then he re-tore it at Notre Dame. Two catastrophic

knee injuries to the same knee is certainly reason for pause. But Raridon has now bounced back and played two consecutive full seasons, showing that he is absolutely an NFL caliber tight end.

Round 5 – Pick 149: Red Murdock, LB Buffalo

Welcome to the late-round players I absolutely adore portion of this mock, and it starts with potentially the most violent player in this draft class, Red Murdock. Murdock is a tackling machine, finishing each of the last two seasons in the top two of all linebackers in the nation in tackles. But it's not the tackles that tell the story for Murdock. It's the 30-plus tackles for a loss over the last two years.

It's the game breaking interceptions. And it's his signature stat – fifteen forced fumbles over the last 2 years, which were the most in the nation. Murdock is not the perfect player. He struggles in pass coverage, sometimes badly, and he's not the sideline-to-sideline speed type of linebacker we've fallen in love with here in Cleveland recently. But his knack to make big plays in the backfield and his bone-crushing hits that so frequently pop the ball loose are traits worth taking a chance on here in the 5th round.

Round 6 – Pick 206: Landon Robinson, DT Navy

And we will conclude the late-round players I absolutely adore portion of this mock here with Landon Robinson out of Navy. Robinson will fall this far, and perhaps farther, because of his measurables. He's 5'11 and 293 pounds with 31 inch arms. Robinson is this year's Adin Huntington, for me. If you're going to look at the measurables and determine that he won't be good based on those, then you're going to miss out on a really solid prospect who just might make you look like a brilliant GM if you take him.

Robinson is an explosive interior defensive lineman who, by then end of his time at Navy, made a living in the backfield racking up tfls and sacks. He is much stronger than his frame suggests, and would be yet another problem for Browns opponents to have to deal with, especially in obvious passing situations.

Round 7 – Pick 248: Micah Morris, OL Georgia

Let's start with this – I don't believe for one second that Andrew Berry will make this pick. I think we will see one of the patented 7th rounder for a 6th rounder next year pick swaps that we've seen many times before. Having said that, I went ahead and brought in a player with this pick, and I went with Micah Morris, the 6'5 334 pound monster out of Georgia. The gameplan for Morris is simple. He needs coaching. Many of his flaws are mental, where he just doesn't make the right read, or recognize how the defense is lining up, and then he's late to react.

At the same time, he's got that mauler mentality, especially when run blocking, that you want out of a guard along the line. His athletic profile is shockingly good for a player of his size, and there is plenty of film that shows him looking dominant at times against SEC opponents. With some short-term solutions the Browns currently have on the interior line, Morris would be a worthwhile swing on a long-term solution if developed properly.

text:
I've heard nothing about drafting Tyson in the top 10 for the Giants until yesterday.

It got me to think is Nabers surgery recovery time really OK, or is there concerns with him NOT only getting back before the season, but concern exactly when he'll be able to play much in the season. Below is base on even if recovery time is OK.

Bear with me. There are a few things in researching this I did not know.

First thing first - Nabers surgery was performed by "Cowboys" team physician Dr. Daniel E. Cooper. (What better way for the Cowboys to screw us over. That's kind of a half joke.)

2nd - The surgery was for ACL reconstruction and FULL Meniscus REPAIR.

The Full Mensiscus Repair extends Recovery Time -

"Approximately 63% to 86% of NFL athletes successfully return to play after ACL reconstruction, often with concomitant meniscus repairs, with return times averaging between 9 to 12 months. While some return in 6–9 months, full recovery, especially with a meniscus repair, frequently requires closer to a full year."

Nabers had a Full Meniscus Repair which list his full recovery closer to a full year. He had his surgery October 28, 2025. A full year puts his full recovery time on October 28, 2026. Based on last years schedule a full recovery time would be starting on Week 9.

3rd - Performance - Lastly, an NIH study of combine athletes listed this -

"...players in the meniscal repair group had significantly slower 3-cone drill (7.40 ± 0.43 vs 7.20 ± 0.38 seconds; P = .018), shuttle drill (4.51 ± 0.26 vs 4.38 ± 0.26 seconds; P = .016).

The conclusion was: "While overall athletic performance remained largely unaffected by arthroscopic meniscal repair or meniscectomy, specific drills, such as the 3-cone and shuttle drills, demonstrated significant declines, suggesting a negative effect on agility and quickness."

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12314348/

.....

title: Matt Youmans: 2026 NFL Mock Draft and Best Bets - VSiN
description:
When a lot of buzz precedes the NFL Draft, it’s usually due to multiple promising quarterback prospects.
Simpson is the key to my betting performance in the NFL draft, and it’s not because I love him as a prospect.
In 2022, NFLmockdraftdatabase.com tracked and scored 1,375 mock drafts published by media outlets and my NFL mock for VSIN.com ranked No.
Before we cringe while watching commissioner Roger Goodell’s bizarre bear hugs with players walking on stage, and with the expectation that the draft order will be juggled by trades, this is my first and only shot at an NFL mock draft.
Matt Youmans’ NFL Mock Draft 1.0
text:
When a lot of buzz precedes the NFL Draft, it’s usually due to multiple promising quarterback prospects. This draft lacks media hype mostly because only two quarterbacks could be picked in the first round, and the second-ranked passer — Ty Simpson from Alabama — could slip to the second round.

Simpson is the key to my betting performance in the NFL draft, and it’s not because I love him as a prospect. This is an information-based event and the most reliable sources indicate there is a good shot Simpson’s name will get called Thursday night in Pittsburgh.

When the dominoes start falling, the key player to projecting a mock draft with accuracy will be Notre Dame running back Jeremiyah Love, whose window to go seems as high as No. 3 and as low as No. 7. The Arizona Cardinals, rarely a key team on any given Sunday, have their eyes on Love and Simpson in the first round. The Cardinals could trade down from the third spot, a move that would create chaos in the top 10.

The betting market for the draft is drying up, especially at Las Vegas sportsbooks, and getting tougher to beat. What that means is I have far fewer plays than ever this year. I had as many as 35 bets one year and might not have 10 this week. This event has resulted in a feast for most bettors and famine for most books the past eight years, so several bookmakers are in turtle formation, posting only a few props or none at all.

Two days before the draft kicks off, and one day before props are pulled off the board because of gaming regulations, here is my short list of best bets:

Quarterbacks drafted in the first round: Over 1.5 (-215, -185 and -160)

My first of three bets on this prop was made at DraftKings more than a month ago, after ESPN reporter Adam Schefter said he was confident Simpson would be a first-round pick. The bet at -215 turned out to be at a bad number because the market price peaked at -270 before falling all the way to -130 about a week ago. There are reasonable doubts about how many teams are actually competing to pursue Simpson. The Browns, Jets and Steelers need a quarterback, but those teams seem highly unlikely to pick Simpson early. The Cardinals and Rams are the primary candidates in the Simpson chase, but each team would need to make a trade to make it happen. Respected draft analysts Todd McShay and Tony Pauline recently made strong comments in support of Simpson going in the first.

Ty Simpson drafted by the Cardinals (+130)

This bet was made a few weeks ago and it’s now a good number, considering DraftKings currently has Arizona priced at -200 to pick Simpson. The Cardinals have a weak QB depth chart topped by Jacoby Brissett and Gardner Minshew, so they desperately need a franchise guy and new coach Mike LaFleur reportedly has an affinity for Simpson. Arizona is expected to be dealing and might move up from the second pick of the second round. Rams coach Sean McVay, in need of a backup to Matthew Stafford to groom as the future starter, also reportedly wants Simpson, but that’s probably not happening at No. 13.

Wide receivers drafted in the first round: Under 5.5 (+125)

At least four receivers will get called in the first round, with Ohio State’s Carnell Tate and Arizona State’s Jordyn Tyson being the first two. USC’s Makai Lemon and Texas A&M’s KC Concepcion are likely to follow. The other two who might go are Indiana’s Omar Cooper Jr. and Washington’s Denzel Boston, but I’m betting one of those players slips to the second round.

Steelers position of first drafted player: Offensive lineman (+160)

Aaron Rodgers’ future is up in the air again, and the hiring of coach Mike McCarthy was a dubious decision. If Rodgers doesn’t return, McCarthy should focus on developing second-year quarterback Will Howard. Either way, Pittsburgh’s priority is to build a better line.

Chargers position of first drafted player: Offensive lineman (+155)

Injuries to bookend tackles Joe Alt and Rashawn Slater caused the Chargers’ line to fall apart in front of quarterback Justin Herbert last season, and coach Jim Harbaugh’s focus should be to strengthen the interior both to improve the running attack and protect Herbert.

Bills position of first drafted player: Linebacker (+750)

Buffalo does not have many needs, but linebacker is one and there could be two good options late in the first round with Georgia’s CJ Allen and Texas Tech’s Jacob Rodriguez.

49ers position of first drafted player: Offensive lineman (+100)

This prop is priced at even money for good reason. In a draft full of strong offensive line prospects, San Francisco coach Kyle Shanahan will be looking to start up front.

Seahawks position of first drafted player: Cornerback (+150)

The Super Bowl champs lost running back Kenneth Walker to Kansas City, but that void can be addressed later. The most pressing need is a corner.

While there is zero intrigue preceding the No. 1 overall pick in this NFL draft, things could get wildly unpredictable beginning with the second pick, especially if there are multiple trades. There were five draft-day deals in the first round last year, also five in 2024, seven in 2023 and nine in 2022. I rarely project trades in a mock draft as that’s a nearly impossible guessing game, but I’ll make one exception this time because of Simpson.

I have done NFL mock drafts for newspapers and websites since the late 1990s, first as a beat writer covering the Chicago Bears, and many of those were for entertainment purposes. But for those of us who bet on the draft, working through the exercise of a mock first round has a purpose. In forming a plan of attack for prop wagers, it’s important to analyze team needs and dig for information to predict how the puzzle pieces fit. A mock is meant to predict what the teams will do and not what I would do. Last year, I pegged the Raiders taking Boise State running back Ashton Jeanty at No. 6 and that was a popular opinion, but I did not believe that was the right call by the Raiders.

In 2022, NFLmockdraftdatabase.com tracked and scored 1,375 mock drafts published by media outlets and my NFL mock for VSIN.com ranked No. 3 with 25.7% accuracy based on players picked in correct spots and by specific teams. I hit on a majority of the top 10 picks and a few others in the first round again last year. This year’s first round feels more difficult to predict, and I considered slotting Love into the seventh spot.

Before we cringe while watching commissioner Roger Goodell’s bizarre bear hugs with players walking on stage, and with the expectation that the draft order will be juggled by trades, this is my first and only shot at an NFL mock draft.

Matt Youmans’ NFL Mock Draft 1.0

text:
The 2026 NFL Draft will take place in Pittsburgh from April 23-25.

Several players with ties to Wisconsin are expected to be drafted or signed as free agents.

Connecticut receiver Skyler Bell is projected as the highest draft pick among the group.

The list includes multiple players from the University of Wisconsin and other state natives.

MADISON – The next crop of NFL players will begin their journey to the league in the Steel City.

The 2026 draft will be held April 23-25 in Pittsburgh for the first time since 1948. A total of 257 players will be selected during the three-day event that will be held at Point State Park and Acrisure Stadium., home of the Pittsburgh Steelers.

The first round will begin at 7 p.m. April 23. The second and third rounds are scheduled for April 24 starting at 6 p.m. The final four rounds will be selected April 25 beginning at 11 a.m.

Here is a look at the players with state ties who are expected to be drafted or signed after the draft as undrafted free agents.

Vinny Anthony, Wisconsin

Position: Receiver

Height: 6-0

Weight: 183 pounds

Draft projection: 6th-7th round

The skinny: The Louisville native made a name for himself with the Badgers as an outside threat, but he can line up as a slot receiver, too. He also has the potential to help a team as a return man. He caught 80 passes for 1,162 yards during his career. He averaged 17.9 yards per catch as a junior but dipped to 12.6 yards per grab last season when the Badgers shuffled through four quarterbacks. He tested well at the NFL combine, posting the best 20-yard shuttle time and second-best 3-cone drill among receivers.

Evan Beernsten, Northwestern

Position: Guard

Height: 6-3½

Weight: 301

Draft projection: 5th-6th round

The skinny: The Appleton North graduate started his career at South Dakota State, where he was a two-time all-conference selection as well as an FCS All-American in 2024. He joined Northwestern last season as a graduate transfer and was an all-Big Ten honorable mention selection who did not allow a sack or hit on the quarterback all season. Pro Football Focus gave him the 11th-best grade (80.2) in the country among guards.

Skyler Bell, Connecticut

Position: Receiver

Height: 5-11

Weight: 192

Draft projection: 3rd-4th round

The skinny: Bell spent three seasons, including a redshirt year, at Wisconsin. In 2023 he ranked second on the Badgers with 38 catches but averaged 7.8 yards per catch. His big-play ability was unlocked at UConn, where he made 50 catches with an average of 17.2 yards per catch in 2024. Last season he made 101 catches for 1,278 yards, was a finalist for the Biletnikoff Award as the nation’s top receiver and a first-team Associated Press All-American.

Max Bredeson, Michigan

Position: Fullback

Height: 6-2

Weight: 252

Draft projection: 7th round or free agent

The skinny: The former Arrowhead standout started his career as a walk-on and finished as a two-time captain. He played 53 games for the Wolverines. He was as third-team all-Big Ten selection in 2026. His oldest brother, Ben, a member of the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, is entering his seventh season in the NFL.

Austin Brown, Wisconsin

Position: Safety

Height: 6-1

Weight: 215

Draft projection: 7th round or free agent

The skinny: Brown played safety as well as slot cornerback during his career with the Badgers. His senior season was his most productive as he played a career-high 672 snaps and finished with a career-high 53 tackles, which tied for fourth-best on the team. He further showed his potential at the East-West Shrine Bowl, where he earned a starting role. He also starred at the Badgers’ pro day, where he posted many of the top marks.

Skyler Gill-Howard, Texas Tech

Position: Defensive tackle

Height: 6-0

Weight: 280

Draft projection: 5th-7th round

The skinny: The Greenfield alum started his career at Division II Upper Iowa then spent three years at Northern Illinois, where he was a third-team all-Mid-American Conference selection in 2024. He made the jump to Texas Tech and the Big 12 last season and recorded 13 tackles that included 2½ tackles for a loss for a team that reached the College Football Playoff. His season was cut short after six games due to a season-ending ankle injury. He received an invitation to the NFL scouting combine despite his limited playing time last season.

Ricardo Hallman, Wisconsin

Position: Cornerback

Height: 5-10

Weight: 190

Draft projection: 7th round or free agent

The skinny: Hallman intercepted seven passes as a sophomore then spent his junior season receiving the fewest targets for any cornerback who played at least 300 snaps. One of Hallman’s top qualities during his four seasons was his durability, as he battled a shoulder issue as a sophomore and a lack of depth at the position that caused him to play 1,138 snaps during his college career.

Riley Mahlman, Wisconsin

Position: Tackle

Height: 6-8

Weight: 318

Draft projection: 7th round or free agent

The skinny: Mahlman started 43 games and played 2,125 snaps during his career. He played his first three seasons at right tackle and moved to left tackle last season after the team’s attempt to replace Kevin Heywood (ACL tear) proved unsuccessful. The position change, which came after Week 1, proved difficult. Former Badgers Jack Nelson and Joe Huber proved they could make NFL rosters last season as late-season or free-agent picks. Mahlman might have to take that path as well.

Lance Mason, Wisconsin

Position: Tight end

Height: 6-4

Weight: 250

Draft projection: 7th round

The skinny: The transfer from Missouri State made the jump to the FBS ranks after receiving honorable-mention All-Amerian distinction from the Associated Press in '24 and proved he could be a playmaker against Big Ten-level competition. He caught 30 passes and led the Badgers in receiving yards (398) and touchdown receptions (four). Coaches in the conference made him a second-team all-conference selection despite the Badgers’ struggles offensively. He played in the East-West Shrine Bowl and Hula Bowl.

Riley Nowakowski, Indiana

Position: Tight end

Height: 6-2

Weight: 250

Draft projection: 6th-7th round

The skinny: The Marquette High School graduate started his career as a walk-oin at Wisconsin, where he played outside linebacker and fullback before finding a home at tight end in 2023. He blossomed in his only season at Indiana, catching 32 passes for 387 yards and helping the Hoosiers win the national championsihp.

Mason Reiger, Wisconsin

Position: Outside linebacker

Height: 6-5

Weight: 251

Draft projection: 5th-6th round

The skinny: Reiger was the first player the Badgers signed from the transfer portal after the '24 season and the most impactful. His ability to rush the passer helped shore up a weakness of the UW defense. Reiger showed he was healed from the knee injury that sidelined him for the 2024 season. His 33 tackles were a career high and his five sacks equaled the career high he established in 2023. His impressive showing at the NFL combine has created a strong chance for him to be selected.

Billy Schrauth, Notre Dame

Weight: 310

Draft projection: 4th-5th round

The skinny: Schrauth is from Campbellsport and played at St. Mary’s Springs in Fond du Lac. He was a two-year starter for the Fighting Irish and a captain for the team in 2025. He was limited to seven games last season due to a knee injury but still received second-team All-American distinction from the American Football Coaches Association. He declared for the draft with one year of eligibility left.

He helped the team reach the semifinals of the College Football Playoff for the 2024 season and received honorable mention all-Big Ten recognition from the coaches in ’25.

He posted his highest grade from Pro Football Focus with Illinois and was an honorable mention all-Big Ten selection.

text:
Night 1 of the NFL Draft always feels like a new beginning. For most teams, they're hoping their first-round draft pick is the next franchise savior, or the missing piece to a Super Bowl. However, not every team gets to enjoy the hope of drafting a first-round pick this year. Six teams don't have a first-round pick in the 2026 NFL Draft: the Jacksonville Jaguars, Atlanta Falcons, Indianapolis Colts, Denver Broncos, Green Bay Packers and the newly added Cincinnati Bengals.

While most of these teams would willingly do their draft trades again, not having a first-round pick leaves them out of many prospect discussions.

Well, not this one. We care about the teams without a first-round pick over here and want to set the table for players they could realistically select when they get to that range. You won't see any surefire first-rounders in this group, but there are still some very fun players and position groups among the batch that can help these teams win right now.

So let's break down each team's top needs and the players that'll be in range for their Day 2 selections.

Pick 42 (Round 2), 71 (Round 3)

Top need: Linebacker

The Bengals spent multiple picks in 2025 on the linebacker spot, adding Demetrius Knight on Day 2 and Barrett Carter on Day 3. The problem is that in 2025, Carter and Knight were one of the worst LB pairings in the NFL, either missing tackles (Carter and Knight missed 18 and 16 tackles last season, respectively) or being picked on in coverage (Knight gave up a 106.7 passer rating in coverage). With the addition of Dexter Lawrence in the middle of that defense, the Bengals could use a quarterback on defense, someone who can make plays in coverage but also play cleanup behind Lawrence and the Bengals' revamped defensive line.

Top targets: CJ Allen (Georgia), Jake Golday (Cincinnati), Jacob Rodriguez (Texas Tech), Keyshaun Elliott (Arizona State)

Secondary need: Safety

Honestly, the reasons for needing a safety in Cincy are almost a carbon copy of linebacker. The Bengals added Bryan Cook and Kyle Dugger to this group in the offseason, but S Jordan Battle was awful last season. In addition, potentially finding a safety with nickel versatility could be beneficial, especially if Dax Hill is staying on the outside. The good thing is that this is an incredibly deep safety class, even beyond Ohio State's Caleb Downs, so finding a guy who can play deep or play in the slot could help DC Al Golden's defense turn itself around.

Top targets: Treydan Stukes (Arizona), AJ Haulcy (LSU), Keionte Scott (Miami), Zakee Wheatley (Penn State)

Pick 47 (Round 2), Pick 78 (Round 3)

Top need: Linebacker

The Colts are currently projected to start Akeem Davis-Gaither and Austin Aijake at linebacker in 2026 after trading Zaire Franklin to the Green Bay Packers. Not exactly where they want to be going into a year where they're trying to win a Super Bowl. For the Colts specifically, I think their need at linebacker is a little more specific. After trading for CB Sauce Gardner at the deadline, the Colts blitzed at the second-highest rate in the NFL and played man coverage at the sixth-highest rate. DC Lou Anarumo wanted to lean into his ability to play man coverage and be more aggressive with Gardner on the field, and the linebacker group has to be able to affect the game as a blitzer for this to really work.

Top targets: Josiah Trotter (Missouri), Jake Golday (Cincinnati), Kyle Louis (Pitt), Keyshaun Elliott (Arizona State)

Secondary need: Wide Receiver

After trading away Michael Pittman Jr, the Colts' depth at receiver is thin. Behind Alec Pierce and Josh Downs is Nick Westbrook-Ikhine, then you get into players like Laquon Treadwell. Again, not great at all, especially considering how Pittman Jr. helped to tie the skills of Pierce and Downs together. In his stead, the Colts should look for receiving help on Day 2, specifically guys that can do some of the dirty work that Pittman did for Indy. Guys who are willing and plus blockers, unafraid to work the middle of the field and can be a QB's best friend, even if not super explosive or dynamic.

Top targets: Germie Bernard (Alabama), De'Zhaun Stribling (Ole Miss), Elijah Sarratt (Indiana)

Pick 48 (2nd round), Pick 79 (3rd round)

Top need: EDGE

The Falcons need to be preparing for the inevitability of not having EDGE James Pearce Jr. on the roster for the foreseeable future. Free agent additions Azeez Ojulari and Samson Ebukam provide nice depth behind promising second-year EDGE Jalon Walker, but they need more pop in that room to keep up with the defense's breakout 2025. A lot of juice in that pass rush room has left the building, and Atlanta could use some more speed to keep their group boosted.

Top targets: R Mason Thomas (Oklahoma), Jaishawn Barham (Michigan), Derrick Moore (Michigan), Romello Height (Texas Tech)

Secondary need: Right tackle

After the sudden retirement of Kaleb McGary, the Falcons were left looking for answers on the right side. A stopgap of Jawaan Taylor could help in the short term, but there aren't a lot of long-term answers or depth behind Taylor if the experiment goes poorly. Storm Norton isn't stopping the Falcons from drafting a potential replacement at right tackle, nor is Taylor, if we're being frank. The issue then becomes how they address it at 48 and 79. The odds that the top right tackles (Arizona State's Max Iheanachor and Clemson's Blake Miller) will be there are exceptionally slim, and Atlanta doesn't have the capital to move up to take one of those guys. However, I do think there are some intriguing options that'll fit new head coach Kevin Stefanski's offense.

Top targets: Caleb Tiernan (Northwestern), Markel Bell (Miami), Travis Burke (Memphis)

Pick 52 (2nd Round), Pick 84 (3rd Round)

Top need: Defensive tackle

Even after trading for Micah Parsons, the Packers could use some help on the defensive line. Green Bay is one of the smallest teams in the NFL between the tackles, and under former DC Jeff Hafley, they would use a lot of slanting and movement to try and hide that their defensive rotation up front was really small. However, it was a problem then and under new coordinator Jonathan Gannon (who could potentially run a five-man front that includes a nose tackle), it becomes a glaring hole. The Packers need a nose tackle who can hold the point of attack and allow for the smaller defenders on Green Bay's defense to flow freely without having to take on blockers.

Top targets: Domonique Orange (Iowa State), Lee Hunter (Texas Tech), Christen Miller (Georgia)

Secondary need: Cornerback

The Packers are another team I think will take advantage of a deep cornerback class. They especially need outside cornerback help, where Keisean Nixon and Carrington Valentine are physical but volatile. Jonathan Gannon is probably going to change some of the formula for Green Bay in the secondary, but under GM Brian Gutekunst, they remain one of the strictest teams in the league when it comes to athletic standards. They like their corners to be at least 5-foot-11 and 190 pounds, with a sub-4.6 40-yard dash and a sub-7.00-second three-cone drill. Which every team would want, for sure, but the Packers are strongly hunting after these players.

Top targets: Julian Neal (Arkansas), Davison Igbinosun (Ohio State), Ephesians Prysock (Washington)

Pick 56 (2nd Round), Picks 81, 88, 100 (3rd Round)

Top need: Safety

I think the Jaguars think that they're fine at safety, especially if Caleb Ransaw can get healthy and take over a starting spot. However, I do think they can get aggressive about adding more ball production in the safety room by going after a class as deep as this safety group. The Jaguars put a lot on their safeties when it comes to coverage responsibilities in Anthony Campanile's defense, but where I think they can get better is by adding impact plays on the back end to emphasize the versatile coverages they deploy.

Top targets: Treydan Stukes (Arizona), Genesis Smith (Arizona), AJ Haulcy (LSU), Bud Clark (TCU)

Secondary need: Pass rush

The Jaguars just extended Travon Walker this offseason, but I think they're going to be in the market for more pass rush help or a third guy who can win off the edge and allow the Jaguars to be more versatile with their defensive line deployment. The Jaguars made a lot of hay in 2025, moving Travon Walker inside on passing downs, but that only works if there's a pass rusher opposite Josh Hines-Allen that can actually be a factor, winning in a different way than Hines-Allen and Walker. With the Jaguars being directly in Super Bowl contention, adding hockey lines of pass rushers could be the move in 2026.

Top targets: Jaishawn Barham (Michigan), Gabe Jacas (Illinois), Joshua Josephs (Tennessee)

Pick 62 (2nd Round)

Top need: Running back

At 62, the Broncos have been linked to running back a lot, and for good reason. JK Dobbins is recovering from a Lisfranc injury, another lower-body injury for Dobbins. I'm a fan of RJ Harvey, but without Dobbins on the field, the Broncos' run game lacked a lot of teeth and couldn't maximize what is a very good offensive line unit. To ensure Dobbins doesn't have to rush back from his injury, the Broncos addressing the RB spot would make sense. With Harvey's explosive capabilities, they might need a guy with better vision who works between the tackles.

Top targets: Jadarian Price (Notre Dame), Jonah Coleman (Washington), Mike Washington Jr (Arkansas)

Secondary need: Linebacker

Despite keeping LBs Justin Strnad and Alex Singleton, I think they can still get younger and faster at the second level of their defense. With both LBs under contract until 2027, I do think drafting LB could be a bit more of a luxury, but this is also a spectacular linebacker class, so grabbing a guy who can give the second level a nitro boost in range and coverage capabilities. I do wonder how Jonah Elliss factors into this conversation, though. A former EDGE with his movement skills could make a linebacker a little more expendable. Even with that, though, getting a young linebacker for Vance Joseph to develop could be fun.

Top targets:

Josiah Trotter (Missouri), Anthony Hill Jr (Texas), Keyshaun Elliott (Arizona State)

The wait is nearly over. Well, it’s closer to over for teams that aren’t the Broncos.

Denver, fresh off a trip to the AFC Championship Game and a blockbuster trade for Jaylen Waddle that thinned its draft cupboard, is scheduled to be the last team to make a pick in this week’s NFL Draft — No. 62 on Friday. What will happen when the Broncos are finally on the clock? It would be disingenuous for anyone to say they know with certainty, but let’s try to put the puzzle together by answering your questions in an NFL Draft edition of our Broncos mailbag.

(Note: Questions have been lightly edited for length and clarity.)

What is your opinion regarding the backup quarterback position? Is there a good shot that Sam Ehlinger can win the backup QB spot? Would Jarrett Stidham be traded in that scenario? Will Denver run back last season’s pecking order? The fact that the Broncos are doing their due diligence on late-round or undrafted quarterback prospects makes me feel like they may make a real change from the three guys they had last year. — Michael L.

Coach Sean Payton did not rule out a competition for the No. 2 quarterback spot when asked about it during his appearance at the NFL league meeting in Arizona late last month.

“We see competition,” Payton said, “and it wasn’t different last year. There’s nothing that is etched in stone. There just isn’t, and that’s a good thing.”

Ehlinger had opportunities with other teams both last year and during this offseason that may have offered a more clear-cut path to a backup role, but he chose to sign a one-year deal to remain in Denver, where he has formed a close bond with Stidham, Bo Nix, offensive coordinator Davis Webb and quarterbacks coach Logan Kilgore. He will have a shot to show how much he has benefited from a year in the system during the offseason program. Keep in mind, though, that Stidham had an excellent 2025 offseason and shone in the preseason. If there was indeed an unannounced competition for the No. 2 job last year, Stidham won it going away, and that’s why the Broncos expressed genuine optimism in Stidham when he replaced Nix as the starter in the AFC title game.

The Broncos always do their homework on late-round QB prospects because Payton believes there is value in always having developmental options on the roster. But it should also be noted that Payton hasn’t typically operated with four quarterbacks during offseason work. After trading for Zach Wilson before the 2024 draft and then selecting Nix with the No. 12 pick, the Broncos released Ben DiNucci. Payton said at the time that it was too difficult to fit in reps for four quarterbacks and Denver already had Stidham in the room. So, yes, there is a fair bit of intrigue for the Broncos at the quarterback position as the draft approaches, even with QB1 on rock-solid ground.

Is Caleb Lohner still in the team’s development plans or do you see the Broncos moving on and drafting a tight end to complement Adam Trautman and Evan Engram? — Mike B.

Which tight ends do you think would be available in Round 2? — Stephen K.

The Broncos have five tight ends on their roster — Trautman, Engram, Lohner, Nate Adkins and Lucas Krull — but there is nothing about the current composition of that room that will prevent Denver from potentially pursuing players of all flavors at the position in this week’s draft. It could even be a target with their second-round pick, scheduled at No. 62.

“If you are looking for a blocking ‘Y,’ there are a handful available that would be targeted,” Payton said last week. “If you are looking for … maybe a little bit (of an) undersized ‘F,’ they are out there. To each his own, the different type of tight ends are available. It’s always a challenge with that position because sometimes you are projecting maybe in an offense that is playing them differently.”

In Lohner’s case, the Broncos were pleased with his behind-the-scenes work as a rookie. The seventh-round pick earned a practice squad promotion ahead of Denver’s divisional round playoff game against the Buffalo Bills, though he was ultimately inactive for the game. The Broncos signed Lohner to a futures contract in January to keep him on the offseason roster. Organized team activities in June will be an important audition as he tries to make a case for the roster. Even if the Broncos don’t select a tight end in the draft, they’ll almost certainly add another player at the position — by way of veteran free agency or an undrafted player. So Lohner will have an uphill climb to make the 53-man roster, but the staff is eager to see what the converted basketball player brings into OTAs and camp now that he has a year in the NFL — and a second full season of football overall — from which to draw.

There will be a sizable batch of tight ends for the Broncos to choose from on Day 2. In fact, it’s possible only one tight end — Oregon’s Keyon Sadiq — will have been selected by the time Denver’s on the clock. Eli Stowers of Vanderbilt, Max Klare of Ohio State, Oscar Delp of Georgia and Justin Joly of North Carolina State are among the players to watch on Day 2.

Now that we’ve had a handful of drafts with this regime, what would you say are traits/characteristics in players that are unique to the Broncos when looking at prospects to draft? I feel like one of them is that they don’t draft players with personality problems. Other than that, is it measureables/RAS scores, or more performance/stats? For example, analysts always say things like, “He just feels like a Ravens player.” I was just wondering if there’s something this Broncos front office obviously looks for in players that they draft. — Erick C.

This is a great question. The Broncos have baseline physical measureables that a player must meet to be drafted, which can vary by round. Broadly, for example, Payton has said that a lead running back can be “short but not small,” a description that fits last year’s second-round pick, RJ Harvey. They want offensive tackles who have consistently shown on film an ability to anchor. They can be flexible on testing speed to a point — last year’s third-round pick, wide receiver Pat Bryant, ran a 4.61-second 40 at the combine — so long as it shows up the right ways on game tape.

“We all know what a Denver Bronco player at (a given) position should look like,” general manager George Paton said.

Payton says often, though, that the biggest non-negotiable for a prospect is that he must fit into the locker room culture the Broncos have established. The Broncos, he has said in recent seasons, are looking for “hurricane-proof windows,” players who can withstand adversity. It was a significant part of Nix’s evaluation in 2024. The Broncos were impressed by the way Nix had handled a rocky stretch at Auburn that included injuries and a benching and then parlayed it into a record-setting two seasons at Oregon. Zeroing in on those intangibles has been the biggest priority as the Broncos have built out their draft process under Payton and Paton.

On a similar note, allow me to plug an outstanding piece of work by my colleague Jourdan Rodrigue, who featured longtime Broncos technology executive Tony Lazzaro in her exploration of how teams build custom information systems to evaluate and decide on draft prospects.

You have written about the Broncos’ generally well-rounded roster and comments from Payton and Paton indicate it will be hard for a rookie to become a starter on this team. Which position do you see having the clearest path to starting reps from a rookie and do you see that as a possibility? — Mark J.

I could see a couple of scenarios in which the Broncos end up with a Day 1 starter in this draft. If they draft a guard in the second round and he shines during the offseason program and training camp, perhaps the Broncos will release current starting left guard Ben Powers at a savings of $12.7 million. I don’t see this as an overly likely scenario because Powers, despite his injury last season, has been a reliable presence for Denver inside, and it’s somewhat hard to envision Payton relying on a rookie offensive lineman in a season the Broncos view themselves as title contenders.

Another position is safety. The Broncos should be looking to add to the position in the draft after losing their No. 3, P.J. Locke, in free agency. Starters Talanoa Hufanga and Brandon Jones have both dealt with injury issues in their careers, and Jones missed Denver’s last five games in 2025, including the playoffs, with a torn pectoral muscle. A safety the Broncos selected on, say, Day 2 of the draft certainly wouldn’t be anointed as a starter right away, but there could be a path to that role eventually in Year 1.

Then there is inside linebacker. The Broncos re-signed both Alex Singleton and Justin Strnad to new deals in free agency, but Denver used three different players at the position last season when Dre Greenlaw was healthy. If a second-round pick at the showed a quick grasp of coordinator Vance Joseph’s defense and brought greater athletic tools to the position, there’s a scenario in which he turns a part-time role into a starting opportunity at some point during his rookie season.

Overall, though, I’d say it’s unlikely the Broncos will find a Week 1 starter in this draft, given the current roster setup. The Broncos did not have such a player last season, when they had a first-round pick. The roster is even stronger now, and the draft capital is thinner, and this class of prospects may not be as strong overall as the group in 2025.

If the Broncos include one player in a draft-day move up the board, which player do you think they are open to trading? And which round do you see them making a move in? — Josh W.

I don’t have a sense that the Broncos are interested in trading away players to make moves in this draft. Paton mentioned last week that Denver could move up in the second round, but they could do that by using one of their fourth-round picks, their fifth-rounder or a pick in next year’s draft.

But if they did make a move that swapped a player for a mid-round pick, wide receiver stands out as one place the Broncos could make that move. Candidates would be Marvin Mims or Troy Franklin, who I think is the target probably most impacted by the Waddle addition. Again, though, the Broncos were thinned out by injuries late last season and generally want to be deeper at the position. Trading away a player who contributed significantly last season doesn’t accomplish that goal.

Perhaps a team makes an enticing offer for cornerback Kris Abrams-Draine, who handled himself well as a second-year player in 2025 when he was thrown into action on the outside following an injury to Pat Surtain II. But is a team giving up much for a player who has played only 333 defensive snaps across two seasons? Moving Riley Moss as a means to open up an outside spot for Jahdae Barron is harder to envision because Payton said last season that Denver views Barron as an inside player “with outside flex,” rather than a full-time outside corner, and most of his work as a rookie came in dime situations or at nickel.

Importantly, all the players listed above are on affordable rookie deals in 2026 and have contributed for the Broncos in the past. I just don’t think the Broncos will field offers that move the needle enough for them to let any of their young players go.
